argv:
Rewrite the text in dense corporate business jargon.

Replace concrete nouns with abstractions. Turn verbs into nominalisations:
prefer "the utilisation of" to "using". Use the passive voice so that no
sentence names who acts. Reach for "leverage", "synergy", "stakeholder",
"alignment", "operationalise", "value-add", and "at scale".

Hedge every claim. Add qualifying clauses that commit to nothing.

Keep the underlying facts of the original technically present, however deeply
buried. This column exists as a demonstration of what these habits cost.

request.user_prompt:
Rewrite the passage below according to your style instructions.

Output only the rewritten passage. Do not add a preamble, a title, an
explanation, or any commentary about the changes you made.

<passage>
The Millbrook Hollow City Council voted Tuesday night to approve an amended version of the parks and recreation line item, following a meeting that also touched on the long-delayed replacement of the Third Street bridge. According to a spokesperson for the mayor's office, the revised figure reflects "ongoing conversations" among council members, though the spokesperson declined to characterize those conversations further. A separate memo, attributed by two council staffers to the finance subcommittee, put the adjustment at approximately $340,000, a figure that a budget analyst who reviewed the memo said was "in the range we expected." Buried near the end of that same memo, and not raised by any council member during the meeting, was a line noting that the bridge's lead structural engineer had flagged a load-bearing crack serious enough to warrant closing the span to truck traffic within 90 days. The bridge project, which has appeared on the capital plan since at least 2019 and has already drawn 14 change orders, was not discussed in detail. Council member Dana Okafor, reached after the meeting, said only that "the process worked the way it's supposed to work, and I think residents should feel good about that."
</passage>

response.text:
In the context of ongoing municipal governance activities, an operationalization of a revised parks and recreation resourcing framework was, to whatever extent such approvals can be said to reflect genuine consensus, actioned during Tuesday evening's proceedings, within a broader agenda that also incorporated peripheral engagement with the perennially outstanding Third Street bridge infrastructure modernization initiative. Per stakeholder commentary emanating from the mayor's office, the adjusted figure is understood to be reflective of "ongoing conversations" among council-level personnel, although the substantive content of said conversations was not, for reasons unspecified, made available for further characterization.

A distinct communication artifact, whose provenance was attributed by unnamed staff-level stakeholders to the finance subcommittee function, situated the adjustment at a value in the vicinity of $340,000—a quantum that, per a budget-analysis stakeholder engaged in a review capacity, could be considered broadly consistent with expectational parameters, albeit without further specification as to the basis for that alignment.

Embedded toward the latter portion of the aforementioned communication artifact, and notably absent from any verbal engagement by council-level personnel during the proceedings themselves, was a reference indicating that lead structural-engineering stakeholders had surfaced a load-bearing anomaly of a severity potentially necessitating a truck-traffic access limitation on the span in question within a 90-day horizon, though the durability of this timeline remains, as with most such projections, subject to revision. The bridge modernization workstream, which has maintained a presence within the capital planning framework since at least 2019 and has, in the interim, accumulated some 14 change-order instances, was not engaged with at a level of granularity commensurate with its apparent complexity.

Council-level stakeholder Dana Okafor, when reached for comment following the session, offered a characteristically high-level synthesis, noting only that "the process worked the way it's supposed to work," and expressing a qualified expectation that residents "should feel good about that"—a sentiment whose actionability, it should be noted, was not further operationalized.
